items.title: You cannot reach absolute zero in finite steps
items.claim: Absolute zero is 0 K, -273.15°C. The third law of thermodynamics says you cannot reach it in a finite number of cooling steps. Modern experiments have got to 38 picokelvin — but the last few degrees stay out of reach forever.

options.text: Equipment cannot handle such low temperatures
Each cooling step removes a smaller and smaller fraction of remaining heat (each reduction of entropy gets harder). Reaching exactly S = 0 would require an infinite number of steps
Heat keeps flowing in from the universe
Atoms melt at very low temperature

items.reveal:
Cooling techniques like adiabatic demagnetisation can lower the temperature of a substance in stages. Each stage requires removing some of the system's entropy. The Nernst-Simon statement of the third law: as T → 0, the entropy of any reversible process approaches a constant, and the rate of cooling per stage falls toward zero.

In practice, the gap from millikelvin to nanokelvin requires entirely different techniques (dilution refrigerators, then laser cooling, then evaporative cooling of trapped atom clouds).

The lowest measured temperature in a lab is about 38 picokelvin (Bremen, 2021). The cosmic microwave background sits at 2.725 K. The coldest natural place known is the Boomerang Nebula at about 1 K.

Even at 0 K, atoms have zero-point motion required by the uncertainty principle — they cannot be truly still.
items.why: Absolute zero is taught as a fixed point on the scale. It is an unreachable asymptote, both thermodynamically and quantum-mechanically.

items.title: Earth's magnetic field is feeble — about 50 microtesla at the surface
items.claim: A typical fridge magnet generates a field of about 5 millitesla at its surface — about 100 times stronger than Earth's field. The field that swings every compass and protects life from solar wind is barely measurable with everyday instruments.
items.prompt: How does such a weak field deflect cosmic rays and the solar wind?

options.text: Charged particles are easily deflected by even weak fields when no other forces apply
Earth's field is much stronger than 50 microtesla in space
The deflection is from the atmosphere, not the magnetic field
The Sun's field cancels in the upper atmosphere

items.reveal_title: Lorentz force on a fast charged particle
items.reveal:
Earth's field at the surface is about 25-65 microtesla, depending on latitude. The field weakens with the cube of distance from the centre (it's nearly a magnetic dipole), so at the magnetopause (about 60,000 km out on the day side) it's down to a few nanotesla.

A proton in the solar wind has speed about 400 km/s. The Lorentz force qv × B is significant: gyroradius (the size of the circular path around a magnetic field line) is about 60 m for a typical solar wind proton near Earth — small compared with planetary scales. So charged particles spiral along field lines rather than crossing them.

The magnetosphere deflects the solar wind around Earth, funnels some particles to the poles (where they collide with the atmosphere and produce auroras), and traps high-energy particles in the Van Allen belts.
items.why: Earth's field 'feels' strong because it moves compasses noticeably. In tesla units it is millions of times weaker than an MRI scanner — but enough to deflect the solar wind.

items.title: Travel fast enough, come home younger than your twin
items.claim: Twin A blasts off at 0.99c, travels to a star and returns. Twin B stays on Earth. When they meet again, Twin A has aged about 4 years while Twin B has aged 28.
items.prompt: Why isn't this paradoxical? Each twin should see the other moving — symmetry would suggest both should age less, not just one.

options.text: They both age the same — special relativity is wrong here

The twin who turns around is the one who accelerates, breaking the symmetry between the two frames; only that twin's worldline is non-inertial, and proper time on a curved worldline between two events is shorter
The travelling twin's clock is broken from acceleration
Gravity from the spaceship slows the travelling twin's biology

items.reveal:
In special relativity, time elapsed between two events depends on the path through spacetime between them. The straight worldline between two events maximises proper time. Any other path (involving acceleration) gives less proper time.

The Earth-bound twin's worldline is approximately straight (inertial). The travelling twin's worldline turns around — it is two straight segments meeting at an angle in spacetime. The two segments sum to less proper time than the straight path.

This is confirmed by atomic clocks flown on planes. Hafele-Keating in 1971 measured nanosecond-level differences that matched relativity's predictions exactly. GPS satellites have to correct for it constantly.
items.why: The 'paradox' is paradoxical only if you forget that one twin accelerates. The two frames are not equivalent.
